items.title: Pure water dissolves more silver chloride than salt water does
items.claim: Silver chloride is famously insoluble — Ksp is about 1.8 times 10 to the minus 10. But it dissolves slightly. Try to dissolve it in salt water and the solubility plummets to almost zero.
items.prompt: Why does adding more Cl- decrease AgCl solubility?

options.text: Le Chatelier — adding more Cl- shifts AgCl(s) is in equilibrium with Ag+ + Cl- back to the left, reducing dissolved Ag+ until [Ag+][Cl-] equals Ksp again
Silver chloride decomposes in salt water
Salt water becomes saturated with itself, leaving no room for AgCl

items.reveal:
Suppose in pure water solubility 's' equals square root of Ksp, around 1.3 times 10 to the minus 5 M for AgCl.

In 0.1 M NaCl, [Cl-] is dominated by the salt (about 0.1 M). [Ag+] must satisfy [Ag+] times 0.1 equals 1.8 times 10 to the minus 10, so [Ag+] is about 1.8 times 10 to the minus 9 M. Solubility drops by a factor of nearly 10,000.

This is exploited in gravimetric analysis: precipitate the analyte by adding excess of a common ion, ensuring almost everything comes out of solution.
items.why: Students think 'dissolved + dissolved = more dissolved'. Le Chatelier flips the intuition for ionic equilibria.

items.title: Gold is yellow because electrons travel near the speed of light
items.claim: Silver, copper and gold are all in Group 11 of the periodic table. Silver is shiny white, copper is reddish-orange, gold is yellow. The colour of gold is a relativistic effect — without Einstein, gold would look silver.

options.text: Gold absorbs light because it is the densest of the three

Gold's 1s electrons move at about 58 percent the speed of light, gaining relativistic mass; this contracts the s-orbitals, raises the 5d level and lowers the 6s level, shrinking the 5d-to-6s gap into the visible (blue absorbed, yellow reflected)
Gold's nucleus emits yellow light when irradiated
Gold's surface oxidises to give a yellow film

items.reveal:
For heavy elements, inner-shell electrons move at substantial fractions of c. Their relativistic mass increase contracts s and p orbitals, while shielded d and f orbitals expand.

For silver (Z=47) the effect is small — the 5s-to-4d transitions sit in the UV, so silver reflects all visible light evenly. For gold (Z=79) the effect is large — the 5d-to-6s transition slides into the visible blue region. Blue is absorbed; the complementary yellow is reflected.

Mercury's liquidity at room temperature has the same root cause: relativistic 6s contraction weakens mercury-mercury metallic bonding.
items.why: The colour of a metal is treated as a fixed elemental property. For heavy elements, it depends on special relativity.

items.title: Doubling the nucleophile can do nothing
items.claim: Double the concentration of OH- in some nucleophilic substitutions and the rate doubles. In others, the rate doesn't change at all. Same reactants, same nucleophile, very different kinetics.
items.prompt: What controls whether the reaction is SN1 or SN2?

options.text: The structure of the substrate — tertiary halides go via a carbocation intermediate (SN1, rate-determining step doesn't involve nucleophile), primary halides go via concerted backside attack (SN2, rate depends on nucleophile)
The solvent — only polar solvents allow SN2
The atomic number of the halide

items.reveal_title: Mechanism is destiny — and rate law reveals mechanism
items.reveal:
Tertiary carbon centres are sterically blocked from backside SN2 attack but they form stable tertiary carbocations on dissociation. So they go SN1: slow ionisation followed by fast nucleophilic capture. The rate law is first order — only in the substrate.

Primary carbon centres can't make a stable carbocation but they're sterically open. They go SN2: concerted, one-step, with inversion of configuration. Rate law is second order: rate proportional to [substrate][nucleophile].

The same product (an alcohol from a halide) hides two completely different mechanisms with different stereochemistry: racemisation (SN1) versus inversion (SN2).
items.why: Rate laws are not just empirical — they are direct readouts of which mechanism is at work.
